intro: Sport is also work. A college player sits in class in the morning and appears on national television at night. A professional player signs a contract that says where they may live and play. For more than 150 years, athletes, owners, colleges, courts and unions have argued over who controls a player's time, name and career.

This unit reads that argument through real papers: a railroad's offer in 1852, the Western Conference rules written in Chicago in 1895, the reserve agreement of 1879, John Montgomery Ward's 1887 essay, Supreme Court rulings from 1922 to 2021, an arbitrator's decision in 1975 and a labor board ruling in Chicago in 2014.

By the end, you will be able to explain what eligibility rules, the reserve clause and free agency are. You can trace how television money changed college sport. You can also compare how courts, unions and lawmakers each changed the rules, and argue from dated documents about who should own a career.
bigQuestion: Who should control an athlete's time, name and career: the school, the club or the athlete?

title: School, Work, and the Clip

chapters.title: College Sport as Two Sentences
chapters.bigQuestion: How did American colleges come to call the same young person both a student and a star who earns the school money?

story.title: One Locker, Two Papers
story.kicker: A glossy media guide and a plain class schedule hang in the same locker.
paragraphs: Picture a locker in a university football building. Taped inside the door is a class schedule: biology at eight, a writing seminar at eleven, a lab on Thursday afternoon. On the shelf above sits the team's media guide, a thick printed book the athletic department hands to reporters. It lists the player's height, weight, hometown and statistics.

The two papers describe one person in two ways. The schedule says student. The registrar keeps it, and it counts credit hours toward a degree. The media guide says performer. The athletic department prints it because television networks and newspapers sell the games to millions of viewers and readers.

Since 1906 a national body, now called the National Collegiate Athletic Association, has written rules meant to keep those two sentences together. Its rule books set grades players must keep, how much aid they may take and how many years they may play. Courts, Congress and the players themselves have argued over those rules for more than a century.

This chapter follows that argument through real places and papers: a lake in New Hampshire in 1852, a hotel in Chicago in 1895, a report printed in 1929, a Supreme Court ruling in 1984 and a labor board hearing in Chicago in 2014. The tension between the two papers in the locker is the history itself.
story.think: If a school earns money when a player appears on television, is that player still only a student? What would you need to know to decide?

lessons.title: A Railroad Pays for a Race, 1852
lessons.mainIdea: The first contest between American colleges, an 1852 rowing race, was already tied to a business that wanted crowds.
reading: On August 3, 1852, rowing crews from Harvard and Yale raced on Lake Winnipesaukee in New Hampshire. Historians count it as the first *intercollegiate* athletic contest in the United States. Harvard's boat won. The students did not organize the trip alone.

A railroad company offered to pay the crews' travel and lodging. Its manager hoped the race would draw passengers to the lake resort along its line. So the very first college contest had a *sponsor*, a business that paid expenses because it expected to profit from the attention.

For the next several decades, students ran college sport themselves. Clubs elected captains, raised money, set schedules and wrote rules in student meetings. Faculty mostly stayed away. That student control would not last once crowds, gate money and injuries grew in the late 1800s.

words.d: between two or more colleges, as in a game played by teams from different schools
a person or business that pays costs for an event in return for attention or profit
a rowing or sailing race, or a series of such races

look.title: Who Paid for the Trip?
look.text: In 1852 two college rowing crews traveled to a New Hampshire lake. A railroad paid their way. The railroad hoped fans would buy tickets to ride out and watch the regatta. The students hoped to win.
look.prompt: Each side wanted something different from the same race. What did each want, and does that pattern still show up in college sport?

check.q: What is counted as the first intercollegiate contest in the United States?
choices: A basketball game in Evanston in 1939
A track meet in Chicago in 1895
check.why: Harvard and Yale rowed on Lake Winnipesaukee in 1852, the first intercollegiate contest.

check.q: Why did a railroad pay for the 1852 race?
choices: It hoped the race would bring it passengers
The state of New Hampshire ordered it
check.why: The railroad sponsored the race to draw paying riders to the lake.

check.q: Who ran most college sport in the decades after 1852?
check.why: Student clubs elected captains, raised money and wrote their own rules.

lessons.title: Faculty Take a Seat, 1869–1895
lessons.mainIdea: As games grew bigger, college faculties and presidents took control of sport away from student clubs.
reading: On November 6, 1869, students from Rutgers and Princeton played a kicking game in New Brunswick, New Jersey. Each side had 25 players, and Rutgers won six goals to four. It is remembered as the first college football game, though its rules looked more like soccer than modern football.

By the 1880s, big games drew thousands of paying fans in cities like New York. Students spent the money, hired coaches and sometimes played men who were barely enrolled. Faculty at several schools formed *athletic committees* to approve schedules and check that players were real students.

In 1892 the new University of Chicago hired Amos Alonzo Stagg to run its athletics. He was given a faculty appointment, not a student job. Historians often point to Stagg as an early example of a coach who was a paid member of the university staff. That change moved sport from the student club into the institution.

words.d: a group of faculty members that oversaw a college's sports teams
the teachers and professors of a college or university
money collected from fans who pay to enter a game

look.title: From Student Clubs to Staff
look.cite: Dates as given in standard histories of college sport, including Ronald A. Smith, Sports and Freedom (1988)
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first student race and the first national college body? What changed in between?

check.q: Which schools played the 1869 game remembered as the first college football game?
check.why: Rutgers and Princeton played in New Brunswick on November 6, 1869.

check.q: Why did faculty form athletic committees in the 1880s?
choices: To approve schedules and check that players were real students
check.why: Growing crowds and money led faculty to take oversight of schedules and eligibility.

check.q: What made Amos Alonzo Stagg's 1892 job at Chicago notable?
choices: He held a faculty appointment to run athletics
check.why: Stagg was a paid faculty member, moving sport inside the university.

lessons.title: A Conference Born in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895 university leaders met in Chicago and formed the Western Conference, later the Big Ten, to write shared eligibility rules.
reading: In January 1895 university presidents met at the Palmer House hotel in Chicago. Purdue's president, James Smart, called the meeting. They agreed on rules for which students could play. Seven schools formed what they called the Intercollegiate Conference of Faculty Representatives, better known as the Western *Conference*.

The seven were the University of Chicago, the University of Illinois, the University of Michigan, the University of Minnesota, Northwestern University, Purdue University and the University of Wisconsin. Each school sent a faculty representative. Its early rules required players to be enrolled students in good standing, not hired outsiders.

The conference later took the name Big Ten. The University of Chicago itself left big-time football. President Robert Maynard Hutchins ended the football program after the 1939 season, and the school withdrew from the conference in 1946. A founding member chose classes over the stadium.

words.d: a group of colleges that agree to play each other and follow shared rules
the rules that decide who is allowed to play
a professor chosen by a school to speak for it in a sports conference

look.title: A Founder Walks Away
look.text: The University of Chicago helped found the Western Conference in 1895. Its coach, Amos Alonzo Stagg, won national fame. Yet in 1939 its president ended football, and in 1946 the school left the conference it had helped start.
look.prompt: What reasons might a university president give for ending a famous team? What would a fan or an alumnus say back?

check.q: Where did university leaders meet to form the Western Conference in 1895?
choices: The Palmer House hotel in Chicago
check.why: The founding meeting was held at the Palmer House in Chicago in January 1895.

check.q: Which Illinois schools were among the seven founders?
check.why: The University of Chicago, the University of Illinois and Northwestern were founders.

check.q: What did Robert Maynard Hutchins do after the 1939 season?
choices: Ended football at the University of Chicago
Moved Chicago into the Ivy League
check.why: Hutchins ended Chicago's football program after 1939; the school left the conference in 1946.

lessons.title: A National Body, 1906
lessons.mainIdea: The NCAA began in 1906 as a rules body for football and grew into the keeper of college eligibility.
reading: Football injuries and deaths in 1905 led to a crisis. In December 1905 Henry MacCracken, chancellor of New York University, called colleges to meet. On March 31, 1906, sixty-two schools formed the Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States, or *IAAUS*. It renamed itself the *National Collegiate Athletic Association* in 1910.

At first the NCAA had little power. It published rules for games and passed resolutions about good conduct. But each college still decided for itself who could play. The NCAA asked schools to follow the principle of *home rule*, meaning local faculty enforced standards on their own campus.

The NCAA held its first national championship in track and field in 1921. Championships gave it a reason to set national rules, because every team entering had to meet the same standard. Over time the body that once only wrote rules for games also wrote rules about players' grades, aid and years of play.

words.d: the Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States, founded in 1906 and renamed the NCAA in 1910
the NCAA, the main national body that governs college sport in the United States
the early NCAA idea that each college enforced standards on its own campus

look.title: A Rules Body with No Police
look.text: In its first years the NCAA wrote rules but could not punish a school that broke them. Each campus checked its own players. A college that wanted to win could look the other way.
look.prompt: What problems could home rule cause? What would a national body need before it could enforce its own rules?

check.q: What was the NCAA called when it was founded in 1906?
choices: The Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States
check.why: It began as the IAAUS on March 31, 1906, and became the NCAA in 1910.

check.q: What did home rule mean in the early NCAA?
choices: The national office picked every player
Each college enforced standards on its own campus
check.why: Under home rule, local faculty enforced eligibility themselves.

check.q: Why did national championships push the NCAA toward national rules?
choices: Every entering team had to meet the same standard
check.why: A shared championship needs one standard for every team that enters.

lessons.title: The 1929 Carnegie Report
lessons.mainIdea: A 1929 study by the Carnegie Foundation found that many colleges secretly paid and recruited athletes.
reading: In 1929 the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching published *American College Athletics*, its Bulletin Number 23. Howard J. Savage led the study. Researchers visited over one hundred colleges and universities in the United States and Canada. They read records and interviewed coaches, students and officials.

The report found widespread *subsidies*: jobs that required little work, loans never repaid and payments from boosters. It described recruiting, meaning coaches and alumni seeking out high school players. It blamed college presidents and faculty for allowing commercial pressure to grow on their own campuses.

Newspapers across the country covered the findings. The report did not create a new rule by itself, because the Carnegie Foundation had no power over colleges. But it gave critics a detailed public record. Later reformers cited it when they argued that college sport had become a business wearing a student's clothes.

words.d: money or help given to someone, here secret pay or favors for athletes
seeking out and persuading players to come to a school
a fan or former student who gives money or help to a school's teams

look.title: What the Investigators Found
look.text: The report said commercialism had brought recruiting and subsidizing of athletes into American colleges. It said the responsibility belonged to college presidents and faculties, who had the power to change it.
look.cite: Howard J. Savage and others, American College Athletics, Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, Bulletin 23, 1929
look.prompt: Why might the report blame presidents and faculty rather than coaches or players?

check.q: Who led the 1929 Carnegie study of college athletics?
check.why: Howard J. Savage led the study published as Bulletin 23 in 1929.

check.q: What does subsidy mean in the Carnegie report?
choices: Secret pay or favors given to athletes
A kind of scholarship for all students
check.why: The report used subsidies for jobs, loans and payments given to athletes.

check.q: Why did the report not change the rules on its own?
choices: The Carnegie Foundation had no power over colleges
check.why: The foundation could only publish findings; colleges and the NCAA made the rules.

lessons.title: Scholarships and Divisions
lessons.mainIdea: In 1956 the NCAA allowed athletic scholarships, and in 1973 it split members into three divisions.
reading: After World War II the NCAA tried a strict limit on aid. Its 1948 rule, nicknamed the *Sanity Code*, allowed aid based on financial need and school grades, not on athletic skill. Several schools said openly they would not obey it. The NCAA could not expel them with enough votes, and it dropped the code in 1951.

In 1956 the NCAA changed course. Members could now give an *athletic scholarship* covering tuition, fees, room, board and books, whatever a player's family income. In 1973 the NCAA limited these scholarships to one year at a time, so a coach could decline to renew one. In 2012 members won the option to offer scholarships for several years.

Also in 1973, the NCAA split its members into three *divisions*. Division I held the largest programs. Division III schools agreed not to give any aid for athletic ability. The split let schools with very different budgets follow different rules under one national body.

words.d: the NCAA's 1948 rule that allowed only need-based aid to athletes; dropped in 1951
school aid given because a student plays a sport, first allowed by the NCAA in 1956
one of three NCAA levels, created in 1973, with different rules on aid and size

look.title: Aid Rules Over Time
look.cite: NCAA legislative history as summarized in NCAA Manual records and standard histories
look.prompt: Which change made aid depend on playing rather than on need? How long did the one-year limit last?

check.q: What did the 1948 Sanity Code allow?
choices: Only aid based on financial need and grades
check.why: The Sanity Code allowed need-based aid, not aid for athletic skill.

check.q: In what year did the NCAA first allow athletic scholarships?
check.why: From 1956 schools could give aid covering tuition, fees, room, board and books.

check.q: What do Division III schools agree to?
choices: Give no aid for athletic ability
check.why: Since the 1973 split, Division III schools give no athletic scholarships.

lessons.title: Grades as a Gate, 1983
lessons.mainIdea: In 1983 the NCAA passed Proposition 48, setting minimum grades and test scores for first-year players.
reading: In January 1983 NCAA delegates voted for a rule known as *Proposition 48*. It took effect for students entering in 1986. A first-year player in Division I needed a minimum grade average in a set of high school *core courses* and a minimum score on the SAT or ACT to play and receive aid.

Supporters said the rule told high schools and players that classes mattered. Critics, including leaders at several historically Black colleges and universities, argued that a fixed test score would fall hardest on Black students from underfunded schools. Some coaches, such as Georgetown's John Thompson, protested publicly in later years.

The rule began a long line of *academic eligibility* standards. The NCAA later changed the required scores and added rules for steady progress toward a degree. Each change reopened the same argument: whether a grade rule protects students or keeps some of them out.

words.d: the NCAA rule passed in 1983 setting minimum grades and test scores for first-year Division I players
required high school classes such as English, math and science that count toward eligibility
rules that make a player's right to compete depend on grades and classes

look.title: Two Views of One Rule
look.text: A college president says: a grade rule shows every athlete that the classroom comes first. A college leader from a historically Black university answers: a single test score measures the high school a student attended as much as the student.
look.prompt: Which facts would help you judge each view? What data would you want to see?

check.q: When did Proposition 48 take effect for entering students?
check.why: It passed in 1983 and applied to students entering in 1986.

check.q: What did Proposition 48 require?
choices: A minimum grade average in core courses and a minimum test score
check.why: It combined a grade average in core courses with a minimum SAT or ACT score.

check.q: What was a main criticism of Proposition 48?
choices: It let too many students play
A fixed test score could fall hardest on Black students from underfunded schools
check.why: Critics, including leaders of historically Black colleges, raised this concern.

lessons.title: Evanston, 1939
lessons.mainIdea: In 1939 college sport met two new stages: the first NCAA basketball tournament and the first televised college football game.
reading: In March 1939 the NCAA held its first men's basketball tournament. Eight teams took part. The final was played at Patten Gymnasium on the Northwestern University campus in Evanston, Illinois. The University of Oregon beat Ohio State. The event lost money in its first year.

That same year, on September 30, 1939, an experimental NBC station in New York, W2XBS, broadcast a college football game between Fordham and Waynesburg. Very few homes owned a *television* set, so almost no one saw it. Still, it is counted as the first televised college football game.

The tournament grew as television grew. The field doubled to 16 teams in 1951 and reached 64 in 1985. CBS began carrying the tournament in 1982. By the 2000s its *broadcast rights* paid most of the NCAA's yearly income, which the body shares out to its member schools.

words.d: a system that sends moving pictures and sound to screens; experimental stations began in the 1930s
the legal right, sold for money, to show an event on radio, television or online
a set of games in which teams are knocked out until one champion is left

look.title: NCAA Men's Tournament Field Size
look.prompt: When did the field grow fastest? What connection might that have to television?

check.q: Where was the final of the first NCAA men's basketball tournament played?
check.why: The 1939 final was played in Patten Gymnasium at Northwestern.

check.q: Which game is counted as the first televised college football game?
check.why: W2XBS in New York broadcast Fordham vs. Waynesburg on September 30, 1939.

check.q: What are broadcast rights?
choices: The legal right, sold for money, to show an event
A player's right to speak to reporters
A school's right to build a gym
check.why: Broadcast rights are sold to networks and bring money to the NCAA and schools.

lessons.title: The NCAA Loses Its TV Plan, 1984
lessons.mainIdea: In 1984 the Supreme Court ruled that the NCAA's control of football television broke antitrust law.
reading: Beginning in 1951 the NCAA controlled which college football games appeared on television. It signed deals with networks and limited how often any one school could appear. Leaders said the limit protected attendance at games. Big football schools said it kept them from selling their own games.

The Universities of Oklahoma and Georgia sued. In *NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma* (1984), the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 2 against the NCAA. Justice John Paul Stevens wrote that the plan was a restraint on trade under the *Sherman Antitrust Act*, the 1890 law against deals that limit competition.

After the ruling, conferences and schools sold their own football games. The number of televised games rose quickly. Money flowed to the conferences with the biggest audiences. Later moves between conferences, such as UCLA and USC joining the Big Ten in 2024, followed those television dollars.

words.d: laws that forbid businesses from joining together to limit competition
the 1890 federal law against contracts and deals that restrain trade
an agreement that limits free buying and selling

look.title: The Court on Amateurism and Money
look.text: The Court agreed that the NCAA had a real interest in keeping college sport amateur and linked to schooling. But it held that limiting how many games could be shown on television did not serve that goal. The plan raised prices and cut output, as a cartel would.
look.cite: NCAA v. Board of Regents of the University of Oklahoma, 468 U.S. 85 (1984), opinion of Justice Stevens
look.prompt: The Court accepted amateurism as a goal but still ruled against the NCAA. How can both be true?

check.q: Which schools sued the NCAA over its football TV plan?
check.why: The Universities of Oklahoma and Georgia brought the case decided in 1984.

check.q: What law did the Court say the TV plan broke?
check.why: The Court held the plan was a restraint of trade under the 1890 Sherman Act.

check.q: What happened after the 1984 ruling?
choices: Conferences and schools sold their own games
College football stopped appearing on television
The NCAA took over all conferences
check.why: Freed from the NCAA plan, conferences and schools made their own TV deals.

lessons.title: A Term Chosen for Court
lessons.mainIdea: The NCAA spread the term student-athlete in the 1950s partly to argue that injured players were not employees.
reading: In 1953 the Colorado Supreme Court decided *University of Denver v. Nemeth*. Ernest Nemeth, a football player who also held a campus job, had been hurt in practice. The court allowed him *workers' compensation*, the payments a state requires employers to give injured workers.

Walter Byers led the NCAA as its first executive director from 1951 to 1987. In his 1995 book *Unsportsmanlike Conduct*, he wrote that the NCAA crafted the term *student-athlete* in response to cases like Nemeth's. The phrase stressed school over work, so players would look less like employees in court.

Later courts often agreed with the NCAA. In Rensing v. Indiana State University (1983), the Indiana Supreme Court denied workers' compensation to a football player left with quadriplegia after a practice injury. The court said he was a student, not an employee. The term had become a legal argument as well as a description.

words.d: the NCAA's term for a college player, stressing that the person is a student first
state-required payments to employees hurt on the job
a person who works for someone else for pay and is protected by labor laws

look.title: One Injury, Two Words
look.text: A college football player is badly hurt at practice. If he is an employee, state law may require payments for his care and lost wages. If he is only a student, the law usually does not. The word on his file changes what he can claim.
look.prompt: Why would an organization care which word describes its players? Use the Nemeth and Rensing cases in your answer.

check.q: What did the court decide in University of Denver v. Nemeth (1953)?
choices: The NCAA must share TV money
An injured player could receive workers' compensation
check.why: The Colorado Supreme Court allowed Nemeth workers' compensation.

check.q: Who wrote that the NCAA crafted the term student-athlete?
check.why: Byers, the NCAA's longtime leader, said so in Unsportsmanlike Conduct (1995).

check.q: What did the Indiana Supreme Court rule in Rensing (1983)?
choices: The player was a student, not an employee
Indiana State must leave the NCAA
check.why: The court denied workers' compensation because it saw Rensing as a student.

lessons.title: A Name, a Likeness, a Union
lessons.mainIdea: From 2009 to 2015, players challenged the NCAA over their images and their status as workers.
reading: In 2009 Ed O'Bannon, a former UCLA basketball star, sued the NCAA. He had seen his likeness in a video game without being paid. In 2014 Judge Claudia Wilken ruled that NCAA limits on pay for a player's *name, image and likeness* broke antitrust law. An appeals court upheld much of her ruling in 2015.

In 2014 Northwestern University football players, led by quarterback Kain Colter, asked to form a *union*. A union is a group of workers who bargain together with an employer. The regional director of the National Labor Relations Board in Chicago ruled that the players were employees and could vote.

In August 2015 the full *National Labor Relations Board* declined to decide the case. It said a union at one private school could upset a league made mostly of public universities, which federal labor law does not cover. The ballots the players cast were never counted, but the Chicago ruling stayed a landmark.

words.d: a person's identity used in ads, games or products; often shortened to NIL
a group of workers who bargain together with an employer over pay and conditions
the federal agency that oversees unions and labor rights for private employers

look.title: A Ballot Box Left Sealed
look.text: In 2014 Northwestern football players voted on whether to form a union. The next year the national board declined the case, and the ballots were never counted. The players' vote still exists, sealed and unknown.
look.prompt: Why did it matter that Northwestern is private while most Big Ten schools are public?

check.q: Why did Ed O'Bannon sue the NCAA?
choices: His likeness appeared in a video game without pay
His team was left off television
check.why: O'Bannon saw his likeness used in a video game and sued in 2009.

check.q: Who led the Northwestern players who sought a union in 2014?
check.why: Quarterback Kain Colter led the Northwestern union effort.

check.q: What did the full NLRB do with the Northwestern case in 2015?
choices: Ruled all college players were employees
check.why: The board declined jurisdiction, so the ballots were never counted.

lessons.title: Alston, NIL and a Settlement
lessons.mainIdea: Since 2021 the Supreme Court, state laws and a 2025 settlement have let college players earn money from their names and from schools.
reading: On June 21, 2021, the Supreme Court decided *NCAA v. Alston*, 9 to 0. It ruled that the NCAA could not cap education-related benefits, such as computers or paid internships, that schools give players. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a separate opinion warning that the NCAA's other pay limits might also break antitrust law.

States moved at the same time. California passed its Fair Pay to Play Act in 2019. Illinois passed the Student-Athlete Endorsement Rights Act, which took effect on July 1, 2021. That day the NCAA adopted an interim policy letting players nationwide earn money from endorsements and appearances, called *NIL* deals.

In June 2025 Judge Claudia Wilken approved the settlement in *House v. NCAA*. The NCAA and the largest conferences agreed to pay former players for past NIL limits. Starting in July 2025, schools could share a capped amount of their athletics revenue directly with players. The two papers in the locker now sat beside a third: a pay record.

words.d: short for name, image and likeness; money a player earns from their identity
an agreement that ends a lawsuit without a full trial
giving part of an organization's income to the people who help earn it

look.title: Steps Toward Paying Players
rows: California Fair Pay to Play Act
look.cite: Federal court records: O'Bannon v. NCAA; NCAA v. Alston, 594 U.S. 69 (2021); House v. NCAA
look.prompt: How many years passed from O'Bannon's suit to schools paying players directly? Which step moved fastest?

check.q: What did NCAA v. Alston (2021) decide?
choices: The NCAA could not cap education-related benefits
The NCAA must end March Madness
Colleges could not sell TV rights

chapters.title: Who Owned a Career
chapters.bigQuestion: How did professional athletes go from being bound to one club for life to choosing where they work, and who fought to change it?

story.title: A Name on a Contract
story.kicker: One sentence in a contract let a club keep a player's name, and trade it, for his whole career.
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, a major league baseball contract held a short paragraph near the end. It gave the club the right to renew the contract for the next year. Owners read that paragraph as renewing itself every year. A player who signed once could belong to that club until it sold, traded or released him.

A player's name on that contract was an asset to the club, like a stadium or a bus. The club could trade the name to a team in another city without asking. The player could refuse to report, but then he could not play professional baseball anywhere in organized baseball. Owners called the system the reserve clause.

In October 1969 the St. Louis Cardinals traded outfielder Curt Flood to the Philadelphia Phillies. Flood had played twelve seasons in St. Louis. He refused to go. On December 24, 1969, he wrote to Commissioner Bowie Kuhn that he was not a piece of property to be bought and sold against his wishes.

Flood's letter began a lawsuit that reached the Supreme Court. He lost it. Yet within six years the reserve clause cracked in a different room: an arbitrator's hearing. This chapter follows how a career became property, and how players won back the right to move.
story.think: What is the difference between a job you can leave and a job you can only leave by quitting the whole profession?

lessons.title: Hulbert's League, 1876
lessons.mainIdea: The National League, founded in 1876 by Chicago's William Hulbert, was built by club owners, not players.
reading: The first professional baseball league, the National Association of Professional Base Ball Players, began in 1871. Players moved freely from club to club, sometimes in the middle of a season. Owners called this *revolving*. Clubs that lost stars also lost fans and money, and some folded before finishing their schedules.

William Hulbert, an executive of the Chicago White Stockings, wanted a league run by owners. On February 2, 1876, club representatives met at the Grand Central Hotel in New York and founded the National League. Hulbert soon became its president. Membership belonged to *franchises*, clubs with the sole right to a city.

The new league promised fans a full schedule, banned gambling and alcohol at games and expelled clubs that broke its rules. It also gave owners, not players, the power to set the terms of work. Players could still move to another club after each season, but owners were already looking for a way to stop that.

words.d: the 1870s word for players jumping from one club to another
a club's right, granted by a league, to be its only team in a city
the owner-run baseball league founded in 1876 and still operating today

lessons.title: The Reserve Rule, 1879
lessons.mainIdea: In 1879 National League owners agreed to reserve five players each, the start of the reserve system.
reading: In September 1879 National League owners met in Buffalo, New York. They agreed that each club could name five players it would *reserve* for the next season. No other club would sign those five. The agreement was kept private at first, but it soon became known and then public league policy.

Owners said the rule would keep salaries down and stop rich clubs from signing every star. Over the 1880s the number of reserved players grew, and by the end of the decade whole rosters were bound. The paragraph that carried the rule into each contract became known as the *reserve clause*.

A reserved player had two choices. He could sign on the club's terms, or he could leave organized baseball. Other leagues joined agreements to honor each other's reserve lists. A *blacklist*, a list of banned players, awaited anyone who jumped. The reserve system rested on owners agreeing not to compete for players.

words.d: to claim a player for the next season so no other club can sign him
a contract paragraph that let a club renew a player's contract year after year
a list of people banned from work, here players shut out for breaking the reserve

lessons.title: Ward and the Players' League
lessons.mainIdea: In 1890 players led by John Montgomery Ward started their own league to escape the reserve clause, and it lasted one season.
reading: John Montgomery Ward pitched and played shortstop for New York, and he earned a law degree from Columbia. In 1885 he helped found the *Brotherhood of Professional Base Ball Players*, an early players' organization. In August 1887 he published an essay in Lippincott's Magazine titled Is the Base Ball Player a Chattel?

A *chattel* is a piece of movable property. Ward argued that the reserve clause, once meant to protect clubs, had become a way to buy and sell players. After owners imposed a salary scale in 1888, the Brotherhood acted. In 1890 its members formed the *Players' League*, with clubs partly run by players and backed by investors.

The Players' League drew many of the best players and fans in its one season. Its eight clubs included one in Chicago, which competed with Hulbert's old White Stockings for fans. Money ran short, and backers made deals with the older leagues. The Players' League folded after 1890, and most players returned to their old clubs under the reserve.

words.d: a piece of movable property that can be bought and sold

words.w: Brotherhood of Professional Base Ball Players

a major league run partly by players, which played one season in 1890

lessons.title: A Federal League and a 1922 Ruling
lessons.mainIdea: In 1922 the Supreme Court ruled that baseball was not interstate commerce, giving it an exemption from antitrust law.
reading: In 1914 and 1915 the Federal League challenged the two existing major leagues. It paid high salaries and did not honor the reserve clause. In Chicago its club, the Whales, played in a new ballpark built by owner Charles Weeghman in 1914. That park is known today as Wrigley Field.

The Federal League folded after 1915. Most of its owners took payments to go away. The owners of the Baltimore club did not, and sued the major leagues under the Sherman Antitrust Act. In *Federal Baseball Club v. National League* (1922), the Supreme Court ruled unanimously against Baltimore.

Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote that exhibitions of baseball were local events, not *interstate commerce*. Travel between states was only incidental, he said. So federal antitrust law did not apply. This *antitrust exemption* left the reserve clause beyond the reach of that law for another half century.

a special rule that frees a business from antitrust laws
a rival major league of 1914 and 1915 that did not honor the reserve clause

lessons.title: Flood v. Kuhn, 1972
lessons.mainIdea: Curt Flood challenged the reserve clause in court and lost 5 to 3 in 1972, but the Court called baseball's exemption an anomaly.
reading: In 1953, in *Toolson v. New York Yankees*, the Supreme Court had kept baseball's exemption. It said Congress, not the courts, should change it. Then in 1957, in Radovich v. National Football League, the Court ruled that pro football did not share baseball's exemption. Baseball stood alone.

Curt Flood filed suit in January 1970 against Commissioner Bowie Kuhn. Former Justice Arthur Goldberg argued his case. Flood sat out the 1970 season rather than report to Philadelphia. He played only briefly again, for Washington in 1971, before leaving the game.

On June 19, 1972, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 3 against Flood in *Flood v. Kuhn*. Justice Harry Blackmun wrote that baseball's exemption was an *anomaly*, an odd exception, but that Congress had let it stand for fifty years. The Court would not overturn its own earlier rulings. Flood lost his case and much of his career.

words.d: something odd that does not fit the usual pattern
an earlier court ruling that later courts usually follow
the top official of a professional league, chosen by the owners

lessons.title: Football's Rozelle Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Pro football limited player movement with the Rozelle Rule until a federal appeals court struck it down in 1976.
reading: Football had no antitrust exemption after Radovich, so it limited player movement differently. In 1963 the National Football League adopted a rule named for Commissioner Pete Rozelle. A player could sign with a new club once his contract ended. But the new club owed his old club *compensation*.

If the two clubs could not agree, Rozelle himself set the compensation, often players or draft picks. Clubs feared giving up too much, so few players changed teams. Players called this free agency in name only. The *Rozelle Rule* worked like a reserve clause by another route.

Tight end John Mackey, president of the NFL Players Association, sued. In *Mackey v. National Football League* (1976), a federal appeals court ruled the Rozelle Rule an unreasonable restraint of trade. The court also said such rules could be lawful if the players' union agreed to them in *collective bargaining*. That idea shaped football labor for decades.

words.d: something given to make up for a loss, here players or picks sent to a player's old club
the NFL rule, adopted in 1963, that made a new club compensate a player's old club
talks between a union and employers to agree on pay and rules for all workers

lessons.title: Marvin Miller and the Union
lessons.mainIdea: Under Marvin Miller, elected in 1966, the Major League Baseball Players Association became a strong union that won grievance arbitration.
reading: In 1966 major league players elected Marvin Miller as executive director of the *Major League Baseball Players Association*. Miller had worked as an economist for the United Steelworkers of America. He visited spring training camps and explained labor law to players who had never seen their full contracts.

In 1968 the union signed the first *collective bargaining agreement* in professional sport. It raised the minimum salary from 6,000 to 10,000 dollars. In 1970 the union won the right to send disputes to a neutral *arbitrator* instead of the commissioner. An arbitrator is a person both sides agree will decide a dispute.

In April 1972 players held the first league-wide strike in major league history, over pensions. It lasted about two weeks and cancelled games at the start of the season. Miller's union now had the tools that Ward's Brotherhood had lacked: a signed contract with the owners and a neutral judge for complaints.

words.d: the union of major league players, led by Marvin Miller from 1966 to 1982
a written contract between a union and employers covering pay and rules
a neutral person both sides agree will decide a dispute
a stop in work by union members to press their demands

lessons.title: The Seitz Decision, 1975
lessons.mainIdea: On December 23, 1975, arbitrator Peter Seitz ruled that the reserve clause bound a player for only one extra year.
reading: Pitchers Andy Messersmith of the Los Angeles Dodgers and Dave McNally, lately of the Montreal Expos, played the 1975 season without signing new contracts. Their clubs renewed their old contracts for that one year. The union argued that after the renewal year, the players were free. It filed a *grievance*.

The case went to arbitrator Peter Seitz. On December 23, 1975, he ruled for the players. The renewal paragraph, he wrote, gave a club one more year, not every year forever. Owners fired Seitz at once. A federal court upheld his decision in 1976, and the owners' appeal failed.

Now both sides had to bargain. The 1976 agreement created *free agency* for players with six years of major league service. After that, a player could sign with any club. Earlier, Catfish Hunter had become a free agent in 1974 when an arbitrator found his owner broke his contract. Hunter signed with the New York Yankees on December 31, 1974.

a player's right to sign with any club once a contract ends
the number of years a player has spent in the major leagues

lessons.title: Basketball and Soccer Follow
lessons.mainIdea: Lawsuits in basketball in 1976 and a European court ruling in 1995 opened free movement in other sports.
reading: In 1970 Oscar Robertson, president of the National Basketball Players Association, sued the NBA. The suit challenged the league's reserve system and a planned merger with the rival American Basketball Association. The case settled in 1976. The *Robertson settlement* opened a path to free agency, and the NBA and ABA merged that year.

English soccer had its own chains. Clubs paid a *maximum wage* of 20 pounds a week until players' union leader Jimmy Hill won its end in 1961. In 1963 a court ruled for George Eastham that the retain-and-transfer system was an unreasonable restraint of trade. Clubs could still demand a *transfer fee* when a player moved.

Jean-Marc Bosman, a Belgian player, could not move to a French club in 1990 because his old club demanded a fee. On December 15, 1995, the European Court of Justice ruled for him. The *Bosman ruling* let players in the European Union move freely when their contracts ended, and it limited quotas on foreign players from EU countries.

lessons.title: Collusion and a Lost World Series
lessons.mainIdea: Owners secretly agreed not to sign free agents in the 1980s, and a 1994 strike cancelled the World Series.
reading: After the 1985, 1986 and 1987 seasons, few free agents got offers from new clubs. The union filed grievances. Arbitrators found that owners had acted in *collusion*, meaning they had secretly agreed not to bid for each other's players. The labor contract forbade clubs from acting together that way.

In 1990 owners agreed to pay 280 million dollars in damages to the players harmed. The case showed that free agency on paper still depended on owners actually competing. It echoed the 1879 reserve agreement in Buffalo, when owners also agreed not to compete for players.

In 1994 owners proposed a *salary cap*, a limit on what each club could spend on players. Players went on strike on August 12, 1994. The rest of the season and the World Series were cancelled, the first World Series not played since 1904. The strike ended in the spring of 1995, and baseball never adopted a salary cap.

a limit on how much a team can spend on player pay

lessons.title: The Curt Flood Act, 1998
lessons.mainIdea: In 1998 Congress passed the Curt Flood Act, giving major league players the same antitrust rights as other athletes.
reading: In Flood v. Kuhn, the Supreme Court had said Congress should decide baseball's exemption. After the 1994 strike, Congress acted. President Bill Clinton signed the *Curt Flood Act* on October 27, 1998. Curt Flood had died in January 1997, before the law passed.

The act says antitrust laws apply to major league baseball's dealings with major league players, as they do in other pro sports. It left the rest of the exemption in place, such as rules on minor leagues, franchise moves and broadcasting. The act was narrow, but it carried Flood's name into federal law.

By then every major American league used a mix of free agency, drafts and caps set by bargaining. The *draft*, in which clubs take turns choosing new players, still bound a young player to one club at first. The question Ward asked in 1887, whether a career belongs to the player or the club, stayed alive in each new agreement.
